pins.kicker: Drink tube frozen on a winter hike?
pins.title: Blow it back
pins.sub: After each sip, blow the water back into the bladder so the tube stays empty. Then tuck the tube under your jacket strap.

pins.title: Keep it liquid
items: Blow the tube clear after each sip
Start with warm, not hot, water
Keep a bottle inside your pack
Wrap a bottle in a spare wool sock
Sip often, before it can freeze
pins.sub: The full cold-weather checklist is in our winter guide.

pins.title: Free entry Nov 11
pins.sub: Entrance fees are waived on this fee-free day (check nps.gov for who qualifies). Snow can close roads and trails, so check each park first.

pins.title: Pack a headlamp
pins.sub: November sunsets come early. Use a headlamp, not your phone light, so your map battery lasts. This one switches on with a wave, gloves on.

pins.title: Bring a dry layer
pins.sub: Sweat cools fast once you stop. Change into a dry top and a warm fleece at the car before the drive home.

pins.kicker: Scraped your palm on the trail?
pins.title: Clean it first
pins.sub: Rinse the grit out with clean water, then cover it with a bandage. See a doctor if it's deep or won't stop bleeding.

pins.title: Break them in
pins.sub: Wear them around town and on short, easy walks first, so any hot spots show up close to home, not at mile five.

pins.kicker: Hurt far from the car on a cold day?
pins.title: Hold your heat
pins.sub: Call for help if you can, put on every layer and get off the cold ground. An emergency bivy keeps your body heat in while you wait.

pins.title: Start with easy trails
pins.sub: 10 beginner-friendly national park day hikes as GPX routes for your phone app, plus a route guide.

pins.title: Log every hike
pins.sub: A printable hiking journal for the trail, miles, weather and a few lines about each hike, so you can find your favorites again.
